opus-5.5.text:
I think the comparison really comes down to who pays for the data and whether the product earns its keep on day one.

With cars, the economics are almost miraculous. A customer buys a vehicle because it already does something valuable: it gets them from A to B. Driver assistance is a bonus on top of that. So every car on the road is essentially a data-collection platform that the customer paid for, drives for free, and maintains themselves. The company gets millions of hours of real-world driving, including all the strange corner cases, at close to zero marginal cost. That flywheel is why autonomous driving data scaled the way it did. The base product was already useful, so the data came along as a byproduct.

Robots are in a completely different position. If you try to sell a humanoid or a general-purpose manipulator that can't really do anything yet, who's going to buy it? A household won't pay tens of thousands of yuan for a machine that stands in the corner. A factory won't deploy something that's slower and less reliable than a person or a fixed automation line. Without a working product, there's no customer, and without customers there's no fleet to collect data. So the "sell first, collect data later" playbook from cars basically doesn't transfer. You'd be asking customers to pay to be your data annotators.

That pushes robotics companies toward expensive alternatives. You hire teleoperators, build data-collection farms, and pay for every hour of demonstration. That cost is real and it doesn't shrink much with scale, because each trajectory needs a human in the loop. Some people say we'll just do that at massive scale, but the unit economics are painful compared with a free fleet of cars.

That's why I've placed a lot of emphasis on synthetic data and simulation. If you can generate large amounts of high-quality training data in simulation, and use real-world data mainly to close the gap and fine-tune, you change the cost structure entirely. The goal is to get the robot good enough, from mostly synthetic data, that it can do some genuinely useful tasks on its own. Once it's useful, even in narrow settings like retail, pharmacies, or certain logistics jobs, customers will pay for it. Then you finally get something like the car flywheel: deployed robots doing real work and generating real data as a side effect.

So to me the key question for robotics isn't "how do we copy the car data model." It's "how do we get to the first truly useful capability cheaply enough that deployment becomes self-sustaining." Until you cross that threshold, the data has to come from somewhere other than paying customers, and simulation is the most scalable answer I see.

r001.rationale: The response says customers pay for cars that serve as data-collection platforms, while the company receives driving data at close to zero marginal cost. This conveys that the data is acquired through a customer-funded product.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the comparison is actually quite revealing once you look at the structure of the two businesses.

With cars, the data collection is essentially free from the company's perspective. Someone pays you two or three hundred thousand yuan for a car, they get a useful product that they drive every day, and in the process of using it, the car is generating data for you. The customer isn't buying the car to help you train your model. They're buying it because they need transportation. So the data is a byproduct of a transaction that already closes on its own. That's why Tesla could accumulate billions of miles of driving data. The business model and the data flywheel are aligned, and the customer subsidizes the data collection without even thinking about it.

Robots are the opposite situation right now. If you sell a humanoid or a general-purpose robot today, it honestly doesn't do very much. It can't fold your laundry reliably, it can't cook, it can't do the things people would actually pay for. So who is buying it? Mostly research labs, universities, a few companies doing demos, some very enthusiastic early adopters. They're buying it for the potential, not for the capability. And that means the volume is small, maybe hundreds or a few thousand units, and the usage is not representative of real-world tasks anyway. A robot sitting in a lab being teleoperated by a grad student does not generate the same kind of data as a car being driven on real roads by a real person for real reasons.

So the economics are fundamentally different. In the car case, the customer pays you and gives you data. In the robot case, you're often effectively paying for the data, either through subsidizing the hardware, or through hiring teleoperators to collect demonstrations, or through building your own data collection operation. The data isn't a byproduct, it's the main cost.

And I think this is why the question of what to sell first matters so much. A lot of teams understand that you need data to get capability, and you need capability to sell at volume, and you need volume to get data. That's a chicken-and-egg problem. The car industry broke this loop because the product was already useful before the autonomy existed. Robots don't have that luxury. The robot without capability is just an expensive metal body.

My view is that the way through is to find a narrow use case where the robot can already deliver value, even a small amount, so that someone is willing to pay for it. Maybe it's a factory doing a very specific, repetitive task. Maybe it's logistics. It doesn't have to be glamorous. But once there's a real customer with a real reason to use the product every day, then the data starts to come naturally, and the flywheel can begin. Trying to skip that step and just sell empty robots to collect data, I don't think that math works. The volume isn't there, and the data quality isn't there either.

So in short, cars taught us that the best data comes from a product people already want. Robots are still trying to earn that first want.

r001.rationale: The response says car data collection is essentially free to the company and that the customer pays for the car while subsidizing data collection, conveying a negative acquisition cost.

astra-6.text:
The key difference is that a car already provides value before you use it to collect data. People buy it because they need transportation, so sales can help fund deployment, and that deployment can generate data to improve the system.

With a robot that has no useful capabilities yet, the economics run the other way. Why would someone pay for it? You may have to subsidize the hardware and pay people to operate it just to collect data. That makes building a large fleet much more expensive.

So I think the starting point is a robot that can do a narrow but useful task. Then customers have a reason to buy it, and you have a way to collect relevant data while delivering value. The data still needs to be useful for learning; simply selling more hardware doesn’t guarantee that.

r001.rationale: The response says car sales can help fund deployment and generate data, but it does not clearly characterize the data acquisition cost as negative.

sol-6.1.text:
The key difference is that a car already delivers value. People buy it to get around, and as they drive, you can collect data that helps improve the system. The customer gets a useful product today, and the company gets revenue plus a way to learn from real-world use.

With a robot that has no useful capabilities yet, that loop is much harder to start. Why would someone pay for it? If you’re asking customers to operate it just to generate training data, you’re effectively asking them to fund your development and do some of the work.

So I think the starting point has to be a narrow task the robot can actually perform, at a price that makes sense for the customer. Then deployment can generate data, the data can improve capability, and better capability can support more sales. Data collection strengthens the economics of a useful product; it doesn’t replace the need for one.

r001.rationale: It says car sales provide the company revenue while also letting it learn from real-world use, conveying that data is acquired alongside revenue rather than at a net acquisition cost.
